newsitem.title: SPAIN: As U.S. clamps down, Europe is smokers' paradise.
newsitem.headline: As U.S. clamps down, Europe is smokers' paradise.

text.p: While smoke-free zones are fast becoming the norm in American cities, much of Europe is still a smokers' paradise offering the freedom to light up in restaurants, offices, factories and even hospitals.
Smoking remains a cherished -- if not sacred -- pastime in most European countries, and the few anti-tobacco laws on the books are widely ignored and rarely enforced.
The trendy cafes of Paris' Left Bank, which by French law should have no-smoking sections, are usually too shrouded in musty Gauloises cigarette fumes for patrons to tell the difference.
Germans, normally so law-abiding that crossing the street against the light can lead to a public berating, think nothing of puffing away in no-smoking areas.
At Spain's government ministries, the clouds of cigarette and cigar smoke are sometimes so thick during press briefings that the no-smoking signs on the walls are barely visible.

While governments have started restricting cigarette advertising and health activists are actively encouraging people to kick the habit, the more militant tactics of American anti-smoking crusaders have not caught on.
Europeans generally regard smoking as a matter for individual choice and think American smokers are being unfairly stigmatised in the name of "political correctness".
"For cultural reasons, we prefer to take a gentler approach," said Maria Angeles Planchuelo, a spokeswoman for the Spanish Association Against Cancer.

If trends continue, Europe's taste for tobacco will be undiminished by the latest development in the U.S. "tobacco wars" -- a landmark accord reached in Washington on Friday that imposes new limits on American cigarette makers.

The U.S. tobacco industry agreed to curb the marketing of cigarettes to children and stop selling cigarettes from vending machines and self-service displays. It will be penalised unless tobacco use by children declines to specified target levels.
In settlement of many legal claims and tobacco-related public health issues, the U.S. industry is to pay $368.5 billion over 25 years.
U.S. tobacco firms have also agreed to make a statement acknowledging the dangers of tobacco.

While the number of American smokers has declined to 25 percent of the adult population, estimates for the 15-nation European Union stand at around 34 percent, down only three percent despite a decade of health campaigns.

On paper, French anti-smoking laws are among the strictest in the world. A 1991 law banned smoking in restaurants, cafes and most public places except in designated smoking sections. But in a country where smoking is considered an inalienable right, such restrictions have gone largely unheeded.

Legend has it that French leader General Charles de Gaulle was a three-pack-a-day smoker who gave it up in 1947 only after waking one night to find his bed on fire. But he allowed his cabinet members to puff away during meetings.

"It's not considered a public health problem," said Pascal Menihan-Cheinin of the French National Committee Against Tobacco Use, which estimates that 60,000 people die each year in France from tobacco-related illness.

Italy's cabinet last year ordered compliance with the country's widely flouted rules against smoking in government offices. To almost no one's surprise, the crackdown failed. The few places where smoking is restricted are those catering to American tourists.
Greece is another country where smoking is big business. Leading the world in per capita tobacco use, the average Greek smoker consumes more than 2,700 cigarettes a year.

The Greek cigarette firm Papastratos is among the major international tobacco companies leading the push into Eastern Europe, where the fall of communism has brought a rise in incomes plus a growing taste for Western brands.

With its lax anti-tobacco laws and heavy-smoking population, Romania is seen as one of the most fertile markets. Western-made cigarettes have always been a status symbol, and in communist times a pack of Kent was as good as hard currency.

But European anti-smoking activists are not giving up hope. Britain's new Labour government last month announced plans to outlaw all tobacco advertising, including sponsorship of sports events, and is pushing for a similar ban throughout the EU.
Tobacco companies are even beginning to face lawsuits seeking damages for cancer, and more health-conscious smokers are switching to low-tar brands.
Across Europe, national leaders have also gotten into the act. Polish Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz announced this year he was giving up smoking to set a good example.
Alain Juppe, France's conservative former prime minister, told his cabinet members to avoid lighting up in public because it was bad for their image.
But Denmark's Queen Margrethe II won't be joining the trend. The chain-smoking monarch made headlines earlier this year after a Swedish columnist criticised her for lighting up in public.
Asked to comment on her "smoking problem" during a news conference last November, she replied tersely: "I have no problem."
